records.title: Reproducible NameError with recursive function in PythonREPL()
records.body:
### System Info

MacOS, Python 3.11.2, langchain 0.0.174

### Who can help?

N/A

### Information

- [X] My own modified scripts

### Related Components

- [X] Tools / Toolkits

### Reproduction

I hit a strange error when using PythonREPL in an agent. It happens with this recursive Python function. It was written by gpt-3.5-turbo and is valid Python:


```py
def fibonacci(n):
    if n <= 1:
        return n
    else:
        return fibonacci(n-1) + fibonacci(n-2)  # <-- this line will trigger the NameError
print(fibonacci(10))
```
Note that everything works as expected for non-recursive functions.

Using this function as string input, I reduced the issue to this minimal example:

```py
from langchain.utilities import PythonREPL

python_repl = PythonREPL()
cmd = "def fibonacci(n):\n    if n <= 1:\n        return n\n    else:\n        return fibonacci(n-1) + fibonacci(n-2)\nprint(fibonacci(10))"
python_repl.run(cmd)
```

> $ python t.py
> NameError("name 'fibonacci' is not defined")

When executed with exec(cmd), it runs as expected. I found that PythonREPL runs the command with exec(command, self.globals, self.locals).

Setting globals & locals in this python_repl instance makes the fragment work as expected:

```py
# [... as before ...]
python_repl.globals = globals()
python_repl.locals = locals()
python_repl.run(cmd)
```
This hack solves it only in the context of this simple example, but not if python_repl added as a tool to an AgentExecutor.

At the core, the issue seems to be caused by Python scopes, but my knowledge of this is not profound enough to fully understand what's happening.

### Expected behavior

I would have expected PythonREPL to accept recursive functions.

records.title: Support Nested Complex ComParams with Recursive Parsing Type
records.body:
<!--
SPDX-FileCopyrightText: 2025 The Eclipse OpenSOVD contributors

SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0
-->

## Description

Refactor complex communication parameter parsing to support nested structures by introducing a recursive value type (Option 1), instead of rejecting `ComParamValue::Complex(_)` inside map values.

Today, `HashMap<String, T>::parse_from_complex` in `cda-interfaces/src/datatypes/com_params.rs` only accepts leaf/simple values and returns an error for nested complex values.  
This change affects com-param deserialization boundaries in:
- `cda-interfaces` (`DeserializableCompParam` + com-param data types)
- `cda-database` (`find_com_param` complex parsing path)
- `cda-core` call sites that currently assume flat `HashMap<String, u32>` (notably DoIP NACK retry mapping)

## Motivation

Nested complex parameters are already representable in the DB model (`ComParamValue::Complex`), but current parsing is flat-only.  
Benefits:
- Correct handling of real nested DB com-param payloads
- Clearer and safer type modeling (tree shape represented explicitly)
- Better maintainability vs. ad-hoc special-casing for each nested scenario
- Reduced parsing ambiguity and improved error context for nested fields

## Proposed Solution

Introduce a recursive wrapper type (example shape: leaf value or nested map), and parse `ComplexComParamValue` recursively.

High-level approach:
1. Add a recursive nested com-param type in `cda-interfaces/src/datatypes/com_params.rs`.
2. Implement recursive conversion from `ComParamValue` (`Simple`/`Complex`) into that type.
3. Keep current flat APIs where needed, and provide helper(s) to flatten or iterate leaves for existing consumers (e.g., DoIP NACK mapping) to minimize immediate breakage.
4. Add tests for:
   - nested success cases
   - mixed leaf/nested payloads
   - malformed nested leaves
   - compatibility with existing flat consumers via helper conversion

## Additional Context

Potential call-site impact if adopted as a breaking type replacement:
- `cda-interfaces/src/datatypes/com_params.rs` (`DoipComParams.nack_number_of_retries`)
- `cda-core/src/diag_kernel/ecumanager.rs` (flat `.iter().map(...)` assumptions)
- `cda-database/src/datatypes/comparam.rs` (`map_nack_number_of_retries` currently leaf-only)
- `cda-interfaces/src/com_param_handling.rs` (provider trait currently returns flat map)

To reduce migration risk, prefer incremental rollout: introduce nested type + adapter helpers first, then migrate consumers in follow-up PRs.

_Originally posted by @theswiftfox in https://github.com/eclipse-opensovd/classic-diagnostic-adapter/pull/315#discussion_r3279204392_

> [!IMPORTANT]
> Make sure to link this issue with the PR for your improvement.

records.title: Subtree authority: a parent key cannot act on its descendants — forcing a per-browser key hoard in the console
records.body:
## Problem (chairman, 2026-08-13)

> "this situation where I have to add a separate 'workspace' for different sub accounts of root and get tokens for them, and I have to redo it on every browser I use is ridiculous. If I'm logged into the root account shouldn't that give me access to every account below it? More generally shouldn't I have access to the entire subtree below any account I've added?"

**Yes — and the console's per-browser keyring exists only because the API cannot do this.** This is an aios issue, not an aios-console one.

## Root cause (confirmed in source)

`aios-console/src/lib/aios/session.ts` states the constraint it is working around:

> *"Multi-tenant model: AIOS keys are scoped to a single account; **a parent key cannot impersonate a child**. So 'switching workspace' means switching which key in the keyring is active. Children are captured into the keyring when minted (their first key is returned exactly once)."*

On the aios side (`src/aios/api/deps.py`): a bearer token resolves to exactly **one** `(account_id, key_id, can_mint_children)` and every resource query is scoped to that single `account_id`. Ancestry is consulted in only one narrow place — `services/accounts.py:79`, a **one-level** parent-or-self check for mint/list-children — never for general resource access.

So:
- a root key cannot read a child's sessions/agents/runs;
- the console compensates by hoarding each child's **first-mint key** in an encrypted cookie keyring — which is *per browser*, hence "redo it on every browser";
- a child key returned "exactly once" means losing the cookie can mean losing console access to that child entirely.

## Proposed fix: subtree authority on the token

A key should be able to act on **any account in the subtree rooted at its own account**, not just its own row.

1. **Resolve an actor + a target.** Auth yields the actor account (from the token). Add an explicit target-account selector — header (`X-AIOS-Account: acc_...`) or query param. Absent selector = act as the token's own account (fully backward compatible).
2. **Authorize by ancestry, not equality.** Permit when `target == actor` **or** `target` is a descendant of `actor`. Needs a real ancestry test — recursive CTE over `parent_account_id`, or a materialized path/closure table if depth grows.
3. **Scope every query to the TARGET account** once authorized, so tenant isolation between siblings is unchanged.
4. **Audit the impersonation.** Every acting-as request logs `(actor_account_id, target_account_id)`. Bind both to contextvars so logs and events show who really acted.
5. **Then delete the keyring.** The console keeps ONE key (the account you logged in as) and switches workspaces by changing the target selector — no per-browser state, no first-mint-key hoarding, no "redo it on every browser".

## Security notes (this is the tier-4 part)
- Downward only. A child key must never reach a parent or a sibling.
- Ancestry must be evaluated **server-side per request**, never trusted from the client.
- Consider whether `can_mint_children` and other capability flags are inherited or must be re-checked on the target.
- Archived/suspended accounts in the chain: does the subtree break at an archived node? (Suggest: yes — an archived ancestor should not confer authority.)
- Blast radius of a leaked root key **grows** with this change (it already can mint children; now it can also read them). Worth pairing with scoped keys that can opt OUT of subtree authority.

## Acceptance
- With only a root key, the console lists and operates every descendant account without any additional token.
- A child key still cannot touch its parent or siblings (regression test).
- Logging in from a fresh browser with the root key alone gives the full workspace list.

Filed from the console side too: the keyring/workspace UI should collapse to a selector once this lands.
